explain.say: Imagine walking across 1,300 kilometres of ice, in winds that freeze your face, to stand where no one had ever stood. In 1911, two teams raced to the South Pole! Look at the two teams on the board.

explain.say: On the left is Roald Amundsen from Norway. Look at his tools: sled dogs and skis. He learned from Inuit people in the Arctic to wear loose fur clothes that keep you warm and dry. Can you find the date he arrived?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Planning and the right tools won

explain.say: 14 December 1911! Now look at the right: Robert Falcon Scott from Britain. His team used ponies and motor sledges, but the ponies struggled and the motors broke in the cold. So the men pulled the heavy sledges themselves. How do you think that felt?

explain.say: Exhausting! Scott's team reached the Pole on 17 January 1912, and found Amundsen's tent and flag already there. On the way back, all five died from cold and hunger, only about 18 kilometres from a food store.

faq.q: Who reached the South Pole first?
faq.a: Roald Amundsen of Norway and four companions, on 14 December 1911. Robert Falcon Scott's British team arrived about five weeks later.
asks: When was the South Pole reached?

faq.q: How did Amundsen win the race?
faq.a: He used sled dogs and skis, wore fur clothing like the Inuit, planned many food stores along the route and travelled light and fast.
They were exhausted from pulling sledges themselves, short of food and fuel, and caught in terrible cold and blizzards on the way back. They died only about 18 kilometres from a supply store.
They carried about 16 kilograms of rocks with fossils of a plant called Glossopteris, showing Antarctica once had forests and a warmer climate.

faq.q: How cold is the South Pole?
faq.a: In summer it is usually about minus 25 to minus 30 degrees Celsius; in winter it can fall below minus 60.
asks: What is the temperature at the South Pole?

facts: Roald Amundsen's team reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911.
Robert Falcon Scott's team reached the Pole on 17 January 1912; all five died on the return journey.
